analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans all oil, gas, and mineral leasing in the Arctic Ocean's federal waters.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: after being referred to the House Natural Resources Committee in June 2023, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently prohibit the Department of the Interior from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea planning areas. It was introduced by Rep. Jared Huffman with 11 original cosponsors on June 12, 2023. It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal and Indigenous communities in Alaska who would bear the brunt of any Arctic spill, along with Americans who value intact ocean ecosystems, gain protection from the risk of oil development in a region where cold, ice, and remoteness make cleanup nearly impossible. Future generations gain from lower cumulative carbon emissions and permanently protected federal waters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal and Alaska communities; ocean ecosystems

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently bars the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea planning areas.
It does this by amending Section 8 of the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, making the ban a matter of statute that no administration could reverse by administrative action alone.
Communities and ecosystems along the Arctic coast would be spared the risk of a spill in an area where cleanup conditions are extreme and response capacity is thin.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to a new drilling frontier and any revenue tied to it; the general public could face slightly higher energy prices from reduced domestic supply over the long run.

drawbacks.text: Prohibiting new leasing forecloses domestic oil and gas production from federal Arctic waters, which could mean less domestic supply and modest upward pressure on energy prices in years when other sources are tight.

The ban is written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself, permanently removing the Interior Secretary's discretion to weigh leasing in the Arctic Ocean against other national interests rather than leaving the decision to elected administrations.
The bill as introduced covered the entire Arctic Ocean planning areas, including any mineral production, not only oil and gas, which opponents of the ban would call overly broad.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of a fragile ocean ecosystem and a modest reduction in future oil supply and spill risk; the cost is forgone domestic oil and gas production, which carries a price and energy-security cost in the short term. Because the bill never received a committee vote or floor action, its merits were never weighed in Congress; the practical result is that federal Arctic waters remain legally open to leasing whenever an administration chooses to offer them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there, with no hearing or vote, until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Huffman introduced the bill on June 12, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill expired with the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025, and was never enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and offshore drilling contractors are better off, since federal Arctic waters remain open to future leasing under existing law, and the 12 House members who sponsored the bill saw their proposal die without a hearing.

for.name: Rep. Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 12, 2023 and led 11 original cosponsors.

for.name: 15 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the remainder of the 118th Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on offshore drilling in federal waters, including the Arctic Ocean, throughout the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — 15 of 216 House Democrats cosponsored, with no Republican support — and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar new federal leases and authorizations for drilling in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, cutting off a prospective frontier of production. It never passed, so the industry retains access to federal Arctic waters. Consumers ultimately pay energy prices that partly reflect restricted domestic supply, but the direct effect falls on producers.

Companies that would have contracted for exploration, seismic work, and drilling in Arctic waters lose the prospect of that business. The industry's interest in opening the area runs against the coastal communities and public lands that bear the spill risk.
